key_insight: A recurrent ASR system naturally organizes linguistic information in a hierarchy that mirrors human auditory cortex: distinct model layers map to distinct cortical regions and jointly encode a parallel progression from acoustic → phonetic → lexical → semantic representations.
problem_solved: Clarifies how hierarchical linguistic representations in engineered speech models correspond to spatially distributed processing in the human auditory cortex, bridging a gap between machine speech representations and neurobiology.
method: Compare internal activations of a recurrent automatic speech recognition (ASR) model with neural recordings from human auditory cortex while participants listened to speech.

Use alignment analyses (layer-to-region mapping, representational similarity and encoding models) to identify which model layers correspond to which cortical sites and which linguistic levels (acoustic, phonetic, lexical, semantic) they encode.
Characterize the parallel progression of information in both systems by tracking how representations evolve across model depth and cortical anatomy.
impact: Provides empirical evidence that modern ASR layers recapitulate brain-like, hierarchical speech processing—useful for model interpretability, brain-informed architecture design, and cross-disciplinary validation between neuroscience and speech technology.
visual_elements: Annotated brain map showing auditory cortical regions color-coded and linked to corresponding ASR model layers.
Side-by-side pipeline diagram with parallel streams: model layers (stacked) and cortical regions (anatomical layout) showing the acoustic→phonetic→lexical→semantic progression.
Representational similarity heatmap or matrix illustrating layer-to-region correspondence strengths.
Layer activation trajectories over time for example utterances, annotated with linguistic labels (phoneme, word, meaning) to show temporal evolution.
paper_title: Parallel hierarchical encoding of linguistic representations in the human auditory cortex and recurrent automatic speech recognition systems
paper_authors: Menoua Keshishian, Gavin Mischler, Samuel Thomas, Brian Kingsbury, Stephan Bickel
